sources.entry: celery - An asynchronous task queue/job queue based on distributed message passing.

summary.one_liner: Celery is a Python distributed task queue that runs work asynchronously on worker processes, passing messages through a broker such as RabbitMQ or Redis.
summary.what_it_does: Lets a client enqueue units of work (tasks) that dedicated worker processes pick up and run, communicating via messages through a broker. Supports multiple workers and brokers for high availability and horizontal scaling. Message transports named include RabbitMQ, Redis, Amazon SQS, and Google Pub/Sub, with experimental support for others including SQLite for local development. Concurrency options are prefork, eventlet, gevent, and a single-threaded solo mode. Result stores include AMQP, Redis, memcached, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, and Google Cloud Storage, and serialization supports pickle, json, yaml, and msgpack with optional message signing. The README also lists client implementations in other languages (node-celery, a PHP client, gocelery, gopher-celery, rusty-celery) and notes integration with web frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI.
use_cases: run background jobs in a Python web app
schedule and distribute long-running tasks across machines
process message queues with multiple workers
offload slow work from request handlers
coordinate asynchronous tasks with retries and high availability
how_to_run: from celery import Celery; app = Celery('hello', broker='amqp://guest@localhost//')
notable: Pluggable brokers, result backends, serializers, and pool implementations
Installable feature bundles via pip extras such as celery[redis] or celery[sqs]
Workers and clients retry automatically on connection loss
Client libraries exist for Node.js, PHP, Go, and Rust per the README
caveats: Windows is not officially supported; the README says it may work but asks users not to file platform issues
Requires Python 3.9+ for v5.6.x; v5.7.x needs Python 3.10 or newer; older Python needs older Celery versions
Some transports and result backends are only experimental
